newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand further liberalises insurance industry.
newsitem.headline: Thailand further liberalises insurance industry.

text.p: Thailand's move to grant 28 new insurance licences is a key step to liberalising the industry but could cause some interim problems as the new firms are integrated, analysts and insurers said on Wednesday.

The Thai government ended a drawn-out process on Tuesday when it granted new licences to 12 life and 16 non-life insurance companies. The issuance is the first of a three-phase plan to liberalise the 101 billion baht ($3.9 billion) industry, which grew by about 15 percent last year.
The winners have been waiting since 1995 as three coalition governments with varying political aims deliberated the issue.
The 28 groups, some of which have foreign partners, are dominated mainly by established business conglomerates, well-known families or tycoons and banks or finance companies.
Analysts said the new companies would help expand the industry and increase competitiveness as Thailand sought to liberalise the sector.
"We're pleased to see the promised liberalisation has actually come through," said John Davidson, Asia regional manager with Commercial Union in Singapore.
"We think that the insurance market will grow substantially as a result," he said. "There will certainly be more opportunities in this market in future."
Industry research shows that emerging insurance markets grow faster and branch out into new product lines sooner once they open to the rigours of fuller competition.
"Some of the companies are likely to get some market niche through innovation," said Peter Francke, president of Ayudhya CMG Life Assurance. "Those companies will add value to the industry."

But he and other insurers said they were worried that other new companies, with little experience or exposure to the industry, might hurt existing firms by poaching trained personnel and copying strategies of the established companies.

"The number of experienced insurance people in the industry is limited," said Nick Helms, general manager for General Accident Insurance (Thailand) Co Ltd. "We are all concerned we might lose key personnel."

Although the government cut the number of new licences from the last administration's plan of 66, industry executives said 28 was still too high for an industry that is still immature despite its double-digit growth.
The life insurance side will be doubled with the addition of 12 new companies, and the 16 new non-life firms will bring the total number to 83.

"The number is more than I would have liked to have had, and it will likely cause a disruption in the short term," said Francke. "But after a year or so some losers may emerge and it may be sensible for some to look at the future in terms of mergers."

Given the recent financial slowdown in Thailand and a liquidity crunch, one obstacle that could weed out some companies was the steep capital requirement of 500 million baht for life insurance companies and 300 million for non-life insurance firms, analysts and insurers said.

"The chances are that two years ago, there were plenty of willing partners ready to get into insurance with capital to spare," said one insurer. "Now in the midst of this financial crisis, who can tell how much the picture has changed?"
